subtype: Approach: setting a simple recurring schedule [Action]
passage:
Hi Gurleen,

I'm glad to be your mentor, and here's what I'd suggest so neither of us keeps rescheduling. Forty minutes on video, every other Sunday at 11. The Friday before, I'll send a short agenda with two or three items, and you add one of yours. At the end of each session we agree on one small task to finish before the next, something that fits into a week, like tidying one section of your portfolio or asking a senior for feedback. Our first is the 14th, the second the 28th. If a Sunday doesn't work, tell me by Thursday and we'll move it by a day, but we'll keep the rhythm. Does that feel manageable alongside your exams?

Naveen

qa.q: How long is each session, and how often do they meet?
qa.a: Each session is forty minutes, held every other Sunday.

qa.q: What does Naveen hope to avoid by proposing a fixed rhythm?
qa.a: Naveen hopes to avoid constant rescheduling, wanting steady progress that neither person has to chase.

qa.q: What could Naveen do if Gurleen keeps missing the small task?
qa.a: Naveen could ask what got in the way and make the task smaller, since a task that fits the week is more likely to be done.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel about the plan alongside exams?
qa.a: Gurleen would probably feel relieved that it is light and predictable, especially as Naveen asks if it is manageable.

grounding: Shows a mentor proposing forty-minute meetings on a fixed rota with an agenda sent beforehand and one small task at the end of each session.

subtype: Approach: setting a simple recurring schedule [Action]
passage: You want to know what finally made mentoring work? A calendar. I'm Nandini, and my first try at mentoring Nilesh was a mess: we'd meet whenever one of us remembered, talk for two hours about everything and nothing, and then not speak for a month. So we fixed it. Every second Sunday, 11 to 11.40, on a video call. Not a minute longer. By Friday night, Nilesh sends me a short agenda: what he did, what he's stuck on, one question. And every call ends the same way: one small task for next time. Last month it was 'rewrite your résumé summary in three lines'. The one before, 'ask your lead for feedback on one pull request'. Small. Doable. We've met eleven times in a row now without missing one.

qa.q: How does Nandini feel about the mentoring now compared with the first try?
qa.a: Nandini feels satisfied and proud of the steady rhythm, after the frustration of the messy first attempt.

qa.q: What else could Nandini and Nilesh add to the routine?
qa.a: They could look back every few months at all the small tasks to see progress and choose a bigger goal.

qa.q: How might the routine feel for Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh knows exactly when they'll meet and what to prepare, so the mentoring feels dependable and less awkward to ask for.

grounding: It shows a mentor and mentee meeting for forty minutes every second Sunday with an agenda shared beforehand and one small task set each time.

subtype: Approach: setting a simple recurring schedule [Action]
passage: I'm Nazia, Nandini's flatmate, and I know every other Sunday by the sound of her laptop at 10.55. She mentors a boy from her old coding bootcamp, and she treats it like a train timetable. On Friday nights I see her read an email from him and scribble on a sticky note, his agenda for Sunday, I think. On Sunday she shuts her door at eleven, and at 11.40 exactly she comes out for tea. Once I heard the end of a call: 'Okay, your task for next time: send one message to a company you like.' Two weeks later I heard him say, on speaker, 'They replied!' She did a small dance in the corridor. I don't know how she feels about it inside, but she hasn't missed a single Sunday in five months.

qa.q: At what time does Nandini come out for tea?
What does Nandini's small dance in the corridor suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt delighted and proud that the mentee's small task paid off.

qa.q: What makes the schedule work, and what could make it even better?
qa.a: The fixed time, the agenda sent ahead and a small task each time; they could also look back at progress every few months.

qa.q: How might the mentee experience the timetable?
qa.a: He knows exactly when help is coming and has a clear task, so progress feels steady and achievable.

grounding: It shows a flatmate watching a mentor keep a fixed forty-minute call every second Sunday, with an agenda beforehand and a small task at the end.
